hints: Recall what first ionisation energy means in words, one mole of gaseous atoms losing one mole of electrons to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
walkthrough:
Picture what first ionisation does**
Think of a single isolated oxygen atom in the gas phase. First ionisation removes the very first, outermost electron from that neutral atom. You are left with a singly charged positive ion, also in the gas phase, plus the electron that was removed.

Write it as a balanced equation**
Put the gaseous oxygen atom on the left and the gaseous ion plus electron on the right: $\text{O(g)} \rightarrow \text{O}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$. Both oxygen species must be (g). The electron is shown as $\text{e}^{-}$ and charge balances, 0 on the left, +1 plus -1 on the right.

hints: Look at the overall height of the bars in Fig. 1.1 from Li to Ne, ignoring the small dips at B and O, and state whether the general trend is an increase or decrease.
Think about what happens to the number of protons in the nucleus as atomic number increases across Period 2.
Consider whether electrons are added to the same shell or a new shell across the period, and what this means for shielding of the outer electron.
walkthrough:
Read the overall trend from the chart**
Ignore the two small drops for now. From Li on the left to Ne on the right the bars get taller overall. So the general trend is that first ionisation energy increases across Period 2.

Track the protons**
Across the period each next element has one extra proton, so nuclear charge increases from $+3$ in Li to $+10$ in Ne. A more highly charged nucleus pulls more strongly on the outer electrons, so more energy is needed to remove one.

Check shielding and distance**
All these outer electrons go into the same $n = 2$ shell, with the same inner $1\text{s}^{2}$ electrons shielding them. Shielding stays approximately constant and atomic radius decreases slightly, so the increased nuclear charge is not cancelled out. The effective attraction increases, giving the general increase in ionisation energy.

Final answer: General trend is an increase across Period 2.
Increasing number of protons / increasing nuclear charge gives increased nuclear attraction for outer electrons.
Electrons are added to the same shell so shielding remains similar.

hints: Identify element A from Fig. 1.1 and compare its outer electron arrangement with nitrogen, noting paired versus unpaired $2\text{p}$ electrons.
Think about what happens to the energy needed to remove an electron when two electrons share the same $2\text{p}$ orbital.
walkthrough:
Spot which element dips**
Bar A is for O, which is lower than N before it. Nitrogen is $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}_{x}^{1}2\text{p}_{y}^{1}2\text{p}_{z}^{1}$ with three unpaired electrons in separate orbitals. Oxygen is $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}_{x}^{2}2\text{p}_{y}^{1}2\text{p}_{z}^{1}$, so one $2\text{p}$ orbital now contains a pair.

Feel the repulsion in the pair**
Two negative electrons forced into the same small orbital repel each other. This spin-pair repulsion pushes the electron to higher energy, so it takes less energy to remove it. This effect is larger than the extra pull from one more proton from N to O, so the ionisation energy drops at oxygen.

Final answer: A is oxygen. Oxygen has a spin-paired electron in a $2\text{p}$ orbital.
Repulsion between the paired electrons makes the electron easier to remove and this outweighs the increased nuclear charge, so first ionisation energy is lower than expected.

hints: Scan Table 1.1 and calculate where the jump is much larger than the others, comparing 3rd to 4th with the earlier steps.
Recall that a large jump means the next electron is removed from a shell closer to the nucleus, so count how many electrons were removed before the jump.
Use the fact that E is in Period 3 to build the full configuration with three outer electrons.
walkthrough:
Hunt for the big jump**
Look at the numbers: $577$ to $1820$ to $2740$ rises gradually, then $2740$ to $11600$ jumps by about four times. After that the rises are gradual again. That tells you the 4th electron is much harder to remove than the 3rd.

Link the jump to shells**
The first three electrons come off relatively easily because they are all in the outer $n = 3$ shell, further from the nucleus and shielded by inner shells. The 4th electron must be taken from the $n = 2$ shell, much closer to the nucleus with less shielding, so far more energy is needed. Three electrons removed before the jump means three outer electrons.

Build the Period 3 configuration**
E is in Period 3, so inner shells are full as $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}^{6}$ and the outer shell holds three electrons as $3\text{s}^{2}3\text{p}^{1}$. The full configuration is therefore $1\text{s}^{2} 2\text{s}^{2} 2\text{p}^{6} 3\text{s}^{2} 3\text{p}^{1}$, which is aluminium.

Final answer: Full electronic configuration of E = $1\text{s}^{2} 2\text{s}^{2} 2\text{p}^{6} 3\text{s}^{2} 3\text{p}^{1}$
Largest jump is between 3rd ($2740 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) and 4th ($11600 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) ionisation energies.
This shows three electrons are in the outer shell, so E is Al in Group 13.
